source.title: Word Boundary Information Isn’t Useful for Encoder Language Models
source.authors: Edward Gow-Smith; Dylan Phelps; Harish Tayyar Madabushi; C. Scarton; Aline Villavicencio

record.file_problem: Not stated; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports downstream task scores at multiple training scales, which bear on downstream performance versus scale, but it does not fit or test the original held-out-loss power laws.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions scaling laws as motivation and reports pretraining/validation-loss plots, but does not fit loss against parameters, tokens, or compute or test extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation. Those losses are not reported numerically in the text. The downstream score rows below bear on V6. Results for the word-boundary variants are not included as separate rows: their purpose is testing ways of encoding word boundaries, not the scaling relationship.
record.test_reason: Scale is not the study's question: it is a tokeniser/word-boundary study. It does report fine-tuned downstream scores for encoder MLM models at 3–4 training scales (5.8M–370M params, ~250M–23B tokens), and the authors comment on how tasks respond to scale. These bear weakly on V6 in a new setting (encoders, pretrain-finetune, English and Finnish). Scale changes parameters, data, steps, batch size and data source together. No fit, extrapolation or loss-to-downstream mapping is attempted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that adding word-boundary information, explicitly, implicitly or at finetuning only, gives no substantial improvement, so encoders do well without it. They add that WordPiece′ gives more morphologically valid tokenisations and better complex-word task performance without harming general tasks. Their only scaling remarks are that Superbizarre is less affected by scale and that tokeniser gaps shrink with scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains encoder MLM models across several scales and evaluates fine-tuned downstream tasks; it does not use the original sources' held-out language-model loss fits or compute-optimal allocation analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream performance differs by task, language, tokenizer, and training scale. In particular, WordPiece′ has a small Finnish NER decline from Low to High, while WordPiece rises.

fits_no_version.finding: The downstream advantage of the morphologically aligned tokeniser (WordPiece′) over WordPiece mostly shrinks as training scale grows, except on Superbizarre (+0.9 still at V High). At V Low, WordPiece would need ~20x the training scale to match WordPiece′ on Superbizarre.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tokeniser-induced downstream gaps shrink with training scale, at task-dependent rates.

record.peer_reviewed: Workshop on Representation Learning for NLP
record.problems: The study does not fit or extrapolate scaling curves. Downstream results are task aggregates, with metrics averaged across datasets for GLUE, Superbizarre, FLOTA, and Finnish sequence classification; pretraining and validation losses appear in plots without numerical values in the text. Training scale varies parameters, data, batch size, and steps together, so their separate effects are not identified.
record.rows_left_out: Results for the modified word-boundary architectures across scales (Table 5 and Figures 9–12) are not listed as separate rows; they test alternative word-boundary methods rather than the scaling relation, and the principal tokenizer scale sweeps are represented in rows r1–r44.

untested.parts: Predictive fits or extrapolation of downstream scores; downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; separate effects of parameters vs data; decoder or generative models; scales above 370M parameters.
Loss power-law fits. Training and validation losses appear only in Figures 7–8, against epochs, without numbers.
Not tested. Shape changes with scale (Table 10) and is not held at a fixed parameter count.

missing.what: The authors' statement that downstream-vs-scale curves are approximately logarithmic in training scale, replotted on a log x-axis. This is the only claim about the functional form of downstream scaling.
The same scale trend for seven word-boundary variants across three scales. Declared in rows_left_out, but it is relevant as replication of the V6 trend.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for V6. There are only 3–4 scale points, and parameters, tokens, steps, batch size, depth/width and data source (Wikipedia vs C4) all change together. The figure losses cannot be read numerically. The record's method_sensitivity contains a factual error about a Finnish NER decline that does not exist.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law fits of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Predictive fitting or extrapolation, downstream scores predicted from pretraining loss, and settings beyond the tested encoder models, languages, tasks, and training scales.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bending of loss curves.

relationships.condition: English GLUE, NER and FLOTA, and Finnish NER and sequence classification, for both WordPiece and WordPiece′ across V Low→V High (Finnish to High)
relationships.reason: Scores rise at every scale step: e.g. GLUE 54.7→83.1 (r1–r4), FLOTA 19.5→55.0 (r25–r28), Finnish NER 72.2→89.9 (r33–r35). The authors describe the curves as roughly logarithmic in training scale. Monotone, not fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Scores increase at every scale step along roughly logarithmic trends, including GLUE from 54.7 to 83.1, FLOTA from 19.5 to 55.0 and Finnish NER from 72.2 to 89.9.

relationships.condition: Superbizarre (classifying standalone complex words) for both tokenisers
relationships.reason: Only ~3 F1 gain over ~64x parameters (65.7→68.6, r17–r20; 66.9→69.5, r21–r24). The authors say this task is far less affected by scaling than by tokeniser choice.
relationships.display_finding: About 64× more parameters increased F1 only from 65.7 to 68.6 and from 66.9 to 69.5, with tokenizer choice having a larger effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: English GLUE, NER, Superbizarre, and FLOTA scores for WordPiece and WordPiece′; Finnish sequence-classification scores for both tokenizers; and Finnish NER scores for WordPiece
reader_labels.reason: Metrics rise at each reported increase in scale for these model/task series (r2-r4, r6-r8, r10-r12, r14-r16, r18-r24, r26-r32, r34-r35, r37, r39-r44). This is evidence of scale-associated improvement, not a test of predictive fits.
